strengths: Provides a principled top-down construction of a Transformer-like architecture from energy minimization on the hypersphere, linking Hopfield energy to attention and feedforward modules.
Derives a symmetric self-attention variant and a feedforward module from explicit energy functions, with skip connections and RMSNorm emerging from the optimization view.

The recurrent-depth design with shared parameters and adaptive step sizes is parameter-efficient and enables test-time compute scaling; empirical energy decrease and rank/angle metrics support the intended token-separation dynamics.
Reports competitive results on Sudoku and CIFAR-10 with fewer parameters, and includes detailed derivations and experimental configurations in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty relative to prior energy-based Transformer derivations, especially CRATE, is limited; the proposed modifications (row/column softmax attention, tied Q/K/V projections) do not clearly establish fundamental advantages.

The 'vanilla Transformer' baselines are not standard: using one-layer trainable parameters iterated for all models makes the Transformer comparison weight-tied/recurrent, so claims against vanilla Transformers are not well supported.

Evaluation is mixed and often weaker than claimed: Hyper-SET underperforms on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-100 classification and on masked image modeling at equal iterations, and only closes the gap after scaling iterations/width, often with more computation.

Missing baselines and ablations: no comparison to Universal Transformer, deep equilibrium models, standard deep Transformers with matched effective depth/parameters, or other recurrent/efficient Transformers; main tables lack statistical significance/error bars.

Interpretability claims are not substantiated: energy decrease and rank/angle metrics do not demonstrate interpretability by construction, and no mechanistic or human-interpretable analysis is provided.

Theoretical guarantees are incomplete: no proof of convergence to stationary points under projected/adaptive updates; learned step sizes can be negative and energy decrease is only empirical; the hyperspherical constraint is enforced heuristically via RMSNorm.
Presentation has numerous typos and clarity issues (e.g., 'Sodomu' for Sudoku, 'Hopfiel', 'hypersphercial', duplicated phrases), and reproducibility is limited by the absence of a code release.

strengths: The paper proposes an interesting top-down energy-based derivation of Transformer-like components from modified Hopfield energy on a hypersphere, with explicit energy functions and gradient derivations.
The recurrent-depth design with learned adaptive step sizes is conceptually appealing for parameter efficiency and test-time compute extrapolation.
The Sudoku extrapolation results and the energy/effective-rank/average-angle analyses provide some empirical evidence that the proposed dynamics encourage token separation in subspaces.
The model shows competitive results in some regimes, particularly CIFAR-10 and Sudoku, while using fewer parameters than some baselines.
The paper is generally well-motivated and connects energy-based learning, Hopfield networks, and Transformer architecture design in a coherent narrative.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the work builds heavily on existing energy-based Transformers, Hopfield-network interpretations, recurrent-depth models, and CRATE-style white-box designs. It does not sufficiently differentiate itself from prior energy-based or recurrent-depth architectures, and key baselines such as Universal Transformer, DEQ, and Energy Transformer are missing.

The theoretical derivation has significant gaps. The hyperspherical constraints are not actually enforced: RMSNorm only approximates the norm constraint, and W/D are learned without guarantees of incoherence or spanning properties. There is no convergence or stationarity proof for the alternating minimization or discretized updates, and the sign of the update is inconsistent with standard self-attention, making the claimed recovery of Transformer components questionable.

The interpretability claim is unsupported. The paper asserts that components are interpretable by construction, but the experiments only measure energy, effective rank, and average angle; there is no human or mechanistic interpretability evaluation showing what the components or learned step sizes actually compute.

Empirical evaluation is limited in scope and scale: Sudoku with 9k examples, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, and small masked image modeling experiments. This is far from the foundation-model scale used to motivate the work, and the results do not consistently support the claim of comparable or superior performance.

Baseline comparisons are problematic. The “Transformer” baselines appear to be one-layer models applied recurrently, not standard deep Transformers/ViTs, and many comparisons are not parameter-matched. This makes the reported gains difficult to interpret.

Critical results underperform: on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100, and masked image modeling, Hyper-SET often lags behind Transformer or requires more iterations/width to merely match it, with worse FID/LPIPS in several settings. The paper overstates the empirical conclusions.

Ablations and analyses are insufficient to isolate the effects of the energy formulation, recurrent depth, adaptive step size, symmetric attention, and parameter tying. It is unclear which design choices drive the observed performance.

The paper has clarity and presentation issues, including typos (“Sodomu”, “Hypersphercial”), repeated phrases, unclear distinctions between layers and iterations, and somewhat confusing equation formatting. These issues hinder reproducibility and understanding.
No code release or sufficiently detailed implementation is provided for a novel architecture with many moving parts, limiting reproducibility.

strengths: The paper proposes a novel energy-based derivation of Transformer-like components, connecting hyperspherical Hopfield energy minimization to self-attention, feedforward, skip connections, and RMSNorm, with recurrent depth as a natural consequence.

The architectural design is parameter-efficient: a single-layer recurrent model can extrapolate to more iterations at test time and achieves strong Sudoku results with fewer parameters than the Transformer baseline.
The empirical analysis of energy evolution, effective rank, and average angle provides useful supporting evidence for the hypothesized token-separation dynamics on the hypersphere.
The paper is generally well written and organized, with derivations and implementation details delegated to appendices.
It makes an interesting conceptual contribution to principled architecture design and could inspire further work on energy-based or recurrent-depth Transformers.
weaknesses: The central claim of comparable or superior performance is not convincingly supported: the proposed model underperforms the vanilla Transformer on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100, and masked image modeling under matched iteration budgets, and only matches performance when scaled to more parameters/compute or more iterations.

Evaluation is limited to relatively small-scale tasks and datasets (Sudoku, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, and masked image modeling); there is no evidence that the approach scales to larger models or more realistic benchmarks, despite the paper's framing around foundation models.

Important recurrent-depth and energy-based baselines are missing, such as Universal Transformer, DEQ, PonderNet, and other looped/recurrent Transformers. The comparison to the standard Transformer is also unclear regarding whether it is recurrent or stacked, making fairness hard to assess.

The theoretical derivation has gaps: the projection matrices are assumed to be orthonormal without explicit statement, the constrained optimization is replaced by an unconstrained gradient step plus RMSNorm, and the exact correspondence to the constrained energy minimization is not rigorously established.

The energy functions appear partly constructed to recover known Transformer components rather than emerging from a single principled objective, which weakens the claimed interpretability by construction. Interpretability is not evaluated quantitatively.

Ablation studies are insufficient: there is no systematic analysis of the adaptive step size, the two energy terms, the symmetric column+row softmax attention, recurrent depth versus layer stacking, or the tied-weight feedforward design.

The symmetric attention modification, using both column-wise and row-wise softmax, is non-standard and may reduce expressivity; the paper does not analyze this trade-off or compare against standard self-attention with properly matched parameter counts.

The feedforward module uses tied weights D and D^T with no bias, which is highly restrictive; the need to scale up M or iterations to match Transformer performance suggests an inherent capacity limitation.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or model release is mentioned, and some experimental configurations (e.g., exact Transformer baseline architecture, parameter-matching details, and compute budgets) are not fully specified.
Statistical significance and variance are rarely reported; many results are averaged over only five runs or a single run, and the differences on some benchmarks are small.

The related work positioning is incomplete: CRATE and sparse rate reduction already derive white-box Transformers from optimization principles, but the paper does not sufficiently differentiate its contribution or compare thoroughly against such alternatives.

strengths: The paper presents a principled energy-based framework that connects maximum likelihood on the hypersphere to two complementary objectives (alignment and uniformity), and derives Transformer components such as symmetric attention, feedforward, residual connections, and RMSNorm from energy minimization.

The proposed Hyper-SET is parameter-efficient due to shared parameters across recurrent iterations, and the paper explores useful variants (linear attention, gated FF) and depth-wise LoRA for scalability.

Experiments cover multiple tasks (Sudoku, CIFAR/ImageNet-100 classification, masked image modeling) with detailed training recipes and configs in the appendix, and show competitive or better results in several settings, especially when parameter count is matched or scaled.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to prior energy-based Transformer derivations (e.g., Energy Transformer, CRATE); the main additions—uniformity energy, hyperspherical constraints, adaptive step sizes—are plausible but not a fundamental departure.

Evaluation is limited and mixed: image classification compares mainly to one-layer/parameter-shared Transformers, masked image modeling lags behind Transformer unless more iterations/width are used, and there is no large-scale, language, or autoregressive evaluation.

Theoretical claims are stronger than the evidence: the MLE justification involves strong assumptions, the constraint enforcement via RMSNorm is approximate, and the 'interpretable by construction' claim is not rigorously measured beyond energy/rank/angle diagnostics.

Scalability remains preliminary (<20M parameters), and the lack of causal structure limits applicability to GPT-style autoregressive models; the conclusion acknowledges these but they are central to the claimed general Transformer design.

Reproducibility is partly supported by appendix configs, but no code release or independent reproduction is provided; some experimental comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples (e.g., parameter matching, one-layer recurrent Transformer baselines).

strengths: The paper proposes an interesting top-down energy-based perspective for Transformer design, combining alignment and uniformity on the hypersphere.

It derives a recurrent-depth parameter-shared architecture (Hyper-SET) and demonstrates parameter efficiency relative to certain baselines (e.g., 0.96M vs 1.79M on CIFAR-10) with competitive results against CRATE and Energy Transformer.
The manuscript includes some theoretical motivation (MLE on the hypersphere), extensive appendix details, and empirical analyses of energy evolution, effective rank, and average angle.
It explores generality through alternative energy functions (linear attention, gated FF) and depth-wise LoRA, which could inspire further work.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and positioning is problematic: the approach is very close to CRATE (sparse rate reduction) and Energy Transformer, both of which already interpret Transformer layers as energy minimization. Differences are incremental; relevant work such as nGPT (hyperspherical normalized Transformer) is not discussed or compared.

The theoretical derivation is not rigorous. The MLE objective (Eq. 1) treats the token representation x as a free variable to maximize, which is conceptually questionable. The proposed energy functions are ad hoc surrogates, not derived from the MLE; E_ATTN minimizing logsumexp does not provably yield uniform distribution, and E_FF is not the negative log-likelihood of a vMF mixture. Constraint handling via RMSNorm is asserted, not justified as a projection or convergence-guaranteed alternating minimization.

The derived attention is a non-standard symmetric operator with shared QKV and two softmax terms, which may substantially restrict expressivity. The paper does not ablate this design against standard Q/K/V projections or analyze its computational cost; the extra softmax and step-size network likely increase compute despite parameter savings.

Evaluation is weak and not comparable to standard baselines. The 'Transformer' baseline is a one-layer recurrent/parameter-shared model, not a vanilla Transformer with independent layers; yet the paper claims competitiveness with vanilla Transformers. Standard ViT and standard Transformer baselines are missing.

Sudoku results (54.7% board accuracy) are far below strong published Sudoku solvers (e.g., recurrent relational networks or SATNet) and omit the recurrent transformer baseline [101] that the authors build on.

Image classification only covers small-scale CIFAR/ImageNet-100; Hyper-SET lags or only slightly surpasses a parameter-shared Transformer, and improvements often rely on more hidden dimensions or parameters. No standard ImageNet-1k or language tasks are tested, limiting impact.

Masked image modeling lags behind the Transformer baseline at equal iterations; it only matches by increasing iterations and FF width, while the Transformer is not scaled to comparable compute. Strong generative baselines are missing.

The alternative design variants perform substantially worse than the base model (e.g., linear attention 84.88 vs 90.11 on CIFAR-10), which undermines the claim of a general and useful design principle. Depth-wise LoRA gains are small and only on a small dataset.

Interpretability claims are overstated. Energy decrease during gradient-based updates is expected, and increases in effective rank/average angle are also observed in a shared-QKV Transformer (Appendix F.3), so these analyses do not uniquely support 'interpretable by construction'.

Clarity and reproducibility issues: typos ('Sodomu' for Sudoku), notation inconsistencies, no code release, and the step-size modulation network adds significant complexity/overhead that is not fully ablated.

The paper overclaims scalability ('arbitrary depth', 'competitive or superior') while only testing up to ~20M parameters and 12-24 iterations; the limitations acknowledge that billion-scale and autoregressive modeling remain untested.

strengths: Introduces a principled top-down framework for Transformer design by formulating token dynamics as maximum likelihood estimation on the hypersphere, with dual objectives of semantic alignment and distributional uniformity.

Derives symmetric attention, feedforward layers, RMSNorm, and skip connections naturally from constrained energy minimization, providing an interpretable, energy-based derivation of Transformer components.

Hyper-SET is compact and recurrent-depth, sharing parameters across iterations, and demonstrates competitive or superior performance on several tasks (Sudoku, CIFAR-100, scaled-up image classification) with fewer parameters than vanilla Transformers.

Shows test-time extrapolation to larger iteration counts and generality to alternative energy functions, yielding novel variants such as linear attention and gated feedforward layers, plus a depth-wise LoRA extension for scalability.
The paper is clearly written, with detailed derivations and experimental configurations in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Empirical results are mixed: Hyper-SET lags vanilla Transformer on CIFAR-10, ImageNet-100 classification, and masked image modeling under matched parameter/compute settings, only surpassing when scaled up. The central claim of 'competitive or superior' performance is therefore not fully supported.

Evaluation is limited to relatively small-scale tasks and does not include autoregressive/language modeling or large-scale benchmarks (e.g., billion-parameter models), which the authors acknowledge as a limitation. This limits the demonstrated significance for top-tier AI venues.

The theoretical derivation relies on simplifying assumptions (e.g., uniform prior on the hypersphere, conditional independence) and does not guarantee energy descent or convergence under learned adaptive step sizes in all cases; the interpretability claims remain somewhat qualitative.

Novelty relative to existing energy-based Transformer designs (e.g., CRATE, Energy Transformer) is moderate; while the hyperspherical energy and dual-objective formulation are new, the overall paradigm of deriving Transformers from energy minimization is not entirely novel.

Ablations and comparisons are somewhat limited: no comparison to other recurrent-depth or parameter-sharing Transformers, and the alternative design variants are mostly self-reported with modest gains, making it difficult to assess their practical value.

The practical impact is uncertain: interpretability and parameter efficiency may not outweigh the performance gaps on standard benchmarks, and the framework has not been tested on broader domains such as NLP or multimodal tasks.
